title: Application Development
intro: This domain tests how Pega applications are structured and built: the studios and low-code approach, layered reuse, center-out design, team roles and collaboration tools, the rule/ruleset/class model behind every application, and how to debug what you build. Expect many questions that hinge on precise vocabulary (pattern vs directed, workspace vs branch, major vs patch).

objectives.objective: Evaluate the benefits of using Pega Platform for creating digital solutions
summary: Pega is a low-code platform: instead of writing code, teams model applications visually and declaratively, so the platform effectively generates the software from the model. Business people and developers share one visual language, which shortens feedback loops, supports agile delivery, and lets one design serve many channels (web, mobile, chatbots, email, robots). Integrations are mapped visually and anything built once can be reused. Both citizen developers and professional developers benefit.

Work is split across studios aimed at different audiences. **App Studio** is the low-code workspace for case design, data and UX, used by business architects, citizen developers and system architects; best practice is to build there unless a feature is only available elsewhere. **Dev Studio** exposes the underlying rule forms for security, reuse, integration, class mapping and advanced SLA settings. **Prediction Studio** serves data scientists building adaptive, predictive and text models. **Admin Studio** is for IT system administrators monitoring the runtime. Every studio shares the same layout: header, navigation pane (explorers) and authoring space; the studio switcher is in the upper-left and a default studio opens at login.
Because App Studio uses business-friendly names, the same concept has two names. Rules are generated automatically behind App Studio configuration using these names.
keyFacts: Low-code means visual and declarative modeling instead of hand-written programming.
Best practice: build in App Studio; move to Dev Studio only when App Studio does not expose the feature.

Dev Studio is needed for advanced SLA options such as initial urgency/delay timers, programmatic interval length, business-day calendars, and escalation actions beyond notifications (reassign, resolve).
Prediction Studio requires the `pxPredictionStudio` portal in the operator's access group.
Admin Studio is for runtime monitoring by IT system administrators.
App Studio navigation: Overview, Case Types, Data, Channels, Library (Reuse Library), Users.
The Application profile tracks features, user stories, bugs and feedback for traceability.
Name mapping: Field = Property, Goal & deadline = SLA, User = Operator, Team = Work Group.
Co-development pattern: a business architect designs views in App Studio, a system architect adds functionality and tests in Dev Studio.

rows: Business architects, citizen developers, system architects
Case types, data, UX, personas, low-code configuration
Rule forms, security, integration, class mapping, advanced SLA, reuse
Adaptive, predictive and text ML models

examTraps: Dev Studio is not the default best-practice place to build just because it is more powerful; start in App Studio.
Runtime monitoring belongs to Admin Studio, not Dev Studio.
A User in App Studio is an Operator in Dev Studio, not an access group; a Team is a Work Group.
Not being able to open Prediction Studio is an access group/portal issue, not a licensing of App Studio issue.

objectives.objective: Explain how the Situational Layer Cake, prescriptive design, studio interoperability, and the Reuse Library support modular enterprise reuse
modules: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
summary: The **Situational Layer Cake** lets an organization reuse common logic while still supporting variations, avoiding both tangled if-then-else logic and many near-duplicate applications. Rules are organized in layers: Enterprise (platform-wide and company-wide assets such as authentication), Division (assets reusable within a division, for example a claims flow), Application (app-specific), and Implementation (deployment-specific customization such as regional regulation or localization). At runtime Pega picks the most specific applicable rule, so upper layers can specialize without disturbing the shared layers beneath them. Reusable features can be packaged as module applications stacked as built-on applications. A well-known example is an insurer consolidating 52 claim systems into one claims platform.

Modular enterprise reuse pays off in every phase (design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance) and follows five principles: Interoperable, Updateable, Configurable, Modular and Governed (typically through a Center of Excellence). Prescriptive design means App Studio guides builders toward proven patterns (prescriptive, model-driven UI) instead of free-form coding.

**Studio interoperability**: Dev Studio is where advanced applications, reusable components and modules, traditional UI, and automated unit testing are built, and where rules are marked as relevant records. App Studio consumes that work without code through AI-assisted development, prescriptive UI, relevant records and Configuration Sets. The **Reuse Library** (App Studio Library) is a central repository of reusable assets, backed by governance: lifecycle management (centralized or federated), a reuse catalog with tagging and search, deployment and maintenance tracking, value measurement (usage/ROI dashboards), and education and advocacy.
keyFacts: Layer cake layers, from shared to specific: Enterprise, Division, Application, Implementation.
Runtime selects the most specific rule available for the situation.
Regional regulation or localization variations belong in the Implementation layer.
Reusable features can be delivered as module applications used as built-on applications.
Five reuse principles: Interoperable, Updateable, Configurable, Modular, Governed.
Dev Studio: reusable components/modules, traditional UI, automated unit tests, marking relevant records.
App Studio: AI-assisted development, prescriptive UI, consuming relevant records, Configuration Sets.
Dev Studio can widen a rule's scope from a case type to the application, division or organization for reuse.
Reuse Library governance includes usage/ROI dashboards (value measurement) and a tagged, searchable reuse catalog.
examTraps: Handling variation with if-then-else conditions inside one rule is exactly what the layer cake avoids.
Copying an application per region is the other anti-pattern; specialize in an upper layer instead.
Configuration Sets and AI-assisted development are App Studio capabilities; building reusable modules and automated unit testing are Dev Studio work.
Know the Reuse Library governance aspects by purpose: catalog = find assets, value measurement = usage/ROI.

objectives.objective: Describe the benefits of using the Center-out architecture
summary: Traditional architectures fail in two ways. Top-down designs start at the channel, so logic gets duplicated in every channel. Bottom-up designs start at the data layer, producing siloed and duplicated data with no single view of the customer. **Center-out** puts the business logic layer at the center: the presentation layer responds dynamically to whichever channel is used, and the data access layer is insulated so that a change of system of record (for example moving from on-premises to cloud) requires no change to the business logic.

Five principles drive center-out: manage intelligence centrally; focus on outcomes and align the process (case management); connect up to the channels/experiences; connect down to the data while keeping logic nimble; and manage variations so the solution is scale-ready (the Situational Layer Cake). The benefits are efficiency (define once), agility (one change applies to all channels), governance (auditing and policy) and scalability (reuse logic for new channels). Model-driven UI completes the picture: the data model and rules generate the UI through reusable patterns, so the UI adapts automatically when rules change.
keyFacts: Top-down = channel-first, logic duplicated per channel.
Bottom-up = data-first, siloed duplicated data, no single view.
Center-out = business logic in the middle, channels above, data access below.
Changing the system of record does not require changing business logic.
Benefits: efficiency, agility, governance, scalability.
The fifth principle (manage variations to be scale-ready) is delivered by the Situational Layer Cake.
Model-driven UI uses patterns (forms, lists, dashboards, case UIs) generated from the data model and rules; it is responsive.

rows: Siloed, duplicated data; no single view
Define once, reuse across channels; data layer insulated

examTraps: Center-out does not mean the UI drives design; channels are connected up to central logic.
Agility in center-out means one change applies to every channel, not that each channel is changed independently.
A system-of-record move affects the data access layer only, not lifecycles or UI.

objectives.objective: Describe the accessibility features included in Pega Platform
summary: Because Pega generates UI centrally from patterns and templates, accessibility is implemented once and propagated everywhere. Pega supports WCAG 2.1 and Section 508. When a central component is updated, every application that uses it becomes compliant without per-screen edits. In Constellation, accessibility is built in by default, and templates handle concerns such as layout, responsiveness and accessibility.
Supporting tools reinforce this: the Themes landing page flags WCAG color-contrast failures, and UX designers on the project team focus on accessibility and consistency.
keyFacts: Supported standards: WCAG 2.1 and Section 508.
Implement once in central UI components/patterns; changes propagate to all apps.
Accessibility is built in by default in Constellation.
Templates handle accessibility along with layout, breakpoints and responsiveness.
The Themes landing page highlights WCAG color-contrast failures.
UX designers are the project role responsible for accessibility and consistency.
examTraps: Fixing accessibility screen by screen is the wrong answer; update the central component.
Accessibility is not an optional add-on to enable per view in Constellation; it is default.

objectives.objective: Define the responsibilities of key roles involved in Pega project delivery
summary: A Pega delivery team mixes client and implementation roles. The **Product Owner** (client business) owns scope and prioritizes requirements for sprints. The **Project Manager** leads the delivery team, handling governance, stakeholder liaison, schedule, budget and scope. The **Scrum Master** runs the ceremonies (sprint planning, sizing, backlog refinement, retrospectives) and removes impediments. **System Architects** (SA, SSA, LSA) configure the application; the LSA imports Blueprint files and configures functional and technical requirements and designs the class hierarchy with project leaders.

**Quality Analysts** build test scripts and scenario tests from user stories. **SMEs** supply operational knowledge and walkthroughs. The **Business Architect** translates needs into functional requirements, workflows, data models and UX. **UX Designers** cover user needs, accessibility and consistency. The **Solutions Consultant** works early in the sales cycle, co-designs a Blueprint with the client and hands it to delivery. Most roles work in App Studio; SAs and QAs use Dev Studio, data scientists use Prediction Studio and IT uses Admin Studio.
keyFacts: Product Owner: client-side, defines scope and prioritizes requirements per sprint.
Project Manager: governance, liaison, schedule, budget, scope.
Scrum Master: ceremonies and removing impediments.
LSA: imports Blueprint files, configures functional and technical requirements, designs class hierarchy.
Quality Analyst: test scripts and scenario tests from user stories.
Business Architect: translates business needs into functional requirements, workflows, data models, UX.
Solutions Consultant: pre-sales, co-designs the Blueprint, then hands off.
SMEs provide client operational knowledge.
examTraps: Prioritizing requirements is the Product Owner, not the Scrum Master or Project Manager.
The Solutions Consultant co-designs the Blueprint but the LSA imports it.
Business Architect (requirements) is not the same as System Architect (configuration).

objectives.objective: Explain the roles of Workspaces and Branches in development
summary: A **workspace** is a private development space tied to one operator (with developer access) and one application. Each operator gets one default workspace per application and can create more. Changes stay private until they are shared (pushed) into a branch. Workspaces are available in App Studio and Dev Studio, are enabled by the EnableWorkspace setting, and let you pick the application layer for new rules. The flow is Workspace, then Branch, then merge into the Application.

A **branch** is a container for rulesets that are changing rapidly; branch rulesets are based on another ruleset and hold rules in active development. Best practice is one branch per feature, merged only when the feature is complete, conflicts are resolved and approval is given. Before merge, the system checks for updated or missing rules. Branch quality metrics give a merge-readiness picture: guardrail score (weighted), total merge conflicts, test coverage (percentage of rules covered and test pass rate), and uncovered rules.

Collaboration is supported by Pulse (posts to users, teams and case stakeholders; developers open it through the developer collaboration toggle in the upper-right of App Studio; users through a Pulse widget the developer adds to the portal or case) with email notifications for mentions, likes and comments, and by hashtags that a Tags widget can display.
keyFacts: Workspace = one operator + one application; private until pushed to a branch.
Default one workspace per operator per application; more can be created.
Workspaces are switched on with the EnableWorkspace setting.
Promotion path: Workspace to Branch to Application merge.
One branch per feature; merge after completion, conflict resolution and approval.
Branch quality metrics: guardrail score, merge conflicts, rules covered % and test pass rate, uncovered rules.
Branch rulesets are based on an existing ruleset.
Replying to a Pulse email notification posts the reply as a comment.

rows: Total conflicts to resolve before merge
Percentage of rules covered and test pass rate
Rules not exercised by any test

examTraps: Workspace changes are not visible to teammates until shared to a branch.
A workspace is not shared by a team; it belongs to one operator and one application.
Long-lived per-developer or per-release branches violate the one-branch-per-feature practice.

objectives.objective: Manage application development with Agile Workbench: user stories, feedback, bugs
summary: Agile Workbench lives in App Studio (Application profile and the Developer Assistant pane, whose tabs are Guidance, Knowledge, Work and Checklists). It organizes the application into a feature map of features and subfeatures; creating a case type automatically creates a feature with the same name.

Work items are Stories (user stories, which can be bulk-uploaded from Excel), Bugs and Feedback. Items move between To do, Doing and Done by dragging. During playback sessions with stakeholders, the team records bugs and feedback directly. Agile Workbench integrates with Agile Studio, Jira and CA Agile Central, and is recommended after a Blueprint import to generate the backlog.
keyFacts: Developer Assistant tabs: Guidance, Knowledge, Work, Checklists.
Creating a case type auto-creates a feature of the same name.
Work item types: Stories, Bugs, Feedback.
Statuses: To do, Doing, Done (drag to change).
User stories can be bulk-uploaded from Excel.
Integrates with Agile Studio, Jira and CA Agile Central.
Use playback sessions to capture bugs and feedback from stakeholders.
examTraps: Agile Workbench is an App Studio tool, not Admin Studio.
A defect found in playback is a Bug; a suggestion is Feedback; new scope is a Story.
It integrates with more than just Agile Studio (also Jira, CA Agile Central).

objectives.objective: Create and maintain rules and rulesets
summary: A rule is an instance of a rule type (a Flow rule models a process). App Studio creates rules automatically: a case type produces a work class, a pyDefault case type rule, a data page and properties; a process becomes a Flow rule; a view becomes a Section rule; a data object produces list, lookup and savable data pages. Modular rules provide versioning (history and revert), delegation (business users change values such as an approval threshold) and reuse; parameterization increases reuse further.

A **ruleset** groups rules (like an album groups songs) and can be shared. Its version is Name:MM-mm-pp (major, minor, patch, each 01–99, starting at 01-01-01). Major versions add substantial functionality (and are created for major platform upgrades), minor versions add enhancements, patch versions fix bugs; older versions should be locked. The ruleset stack is the order Pega searches; each listed version also includes lower minor and patch versions within the same major version, and every application version has its own stack. Names should be meaningful and start with the company plus purpose, must not use a Pega prefix, contain no spaces or special characters, and are at most 32 characters. Develop only in the topmost layer and keep built-on applications locked.

In Dev Studio, rules are created via the Create menu, the App Explorer, a rule reference, Save As or the Records explorer. Save As pre-fills everything but you must change the identifier, the class or the ruleset, otherwise saving fails. Every rule's `.pzInsKey` is built from the rule type's internal name, applies-to class, identifier and creation timestamp in GMT; rule resolution then chooses the right rule at runtime.
keyFacts: Ruleset version format: MM-mm-pp, each segment 01–99, first version 01-01-01.
Patch = bug fix, minor = enhancement, major = substantial new functionality or major upgrade.
Lock older ruleset versions; develop in the topmost layer only.
Ruleset names: company + purpose, no Pega prefix, no spaces or special characters, max 32 characters.
A new ruleset's top-level class inherits from @baseclass.
`.pzInsKey` = rule type + applies-to class + identifier + GMT create timestamp (some types add keys, e.g., Correspondence type).
Save As errors unless identifier, class or ruleset is changed.
The Label entered on a new record generates the identifier.
App Studio view = Section rule; process = Flow rule; case type = work class + pyDefault + data page.
Delegation lets business users change rule values (e.g., an auto-approve threshold) in production.
examTraps: Abbreviated names such as UPTC are discouraged; use descriptive names like UPlusTelcoContracts.
Listing a version in the stack includes lower minor/patch versions of the same major only, never a different major version.
The .pzInsKey does not include the ruleset version or the creating operator.
Unlocking a locked version to fix a bug is wrong; create the next patch version.

modules: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
summary: Classes group rules by purpose: Work classes for case processing, Integration (Int) classes for connectors, and Data classes for data types. A child class inherits its parent's rules; case type classes sit under Work, and a child case type gets a class under its parent's. The hierarchy runs from most to least specific: case type classes, Work, Application, Division/Unit (optional, only when necessary), Organization, other (framework) applications, and Pega base classes. A hyphen separates levels, so TGB-IT-Work is a child of TGB-IT, which is a child of TGB.

**Pattern inheritance** is automatic and based on the class-name prefix; it reuses rules by business suitability. **Directed inheritance** is set explicitly as the parent on the class rule form and is used to reuse Pega standard classes (Work-, Data-) or other applications by functional suitability. Rule resolution searches pattern parents first, then the directed parent (and its pattern parents), repeating up to @baseclass; if nothing is found, an error results. Place reusable rules as high as sensible and parameterize instead of duplicating.

**Relevant records** make Dev Studio rules available to App Studio builders. Fields, views, processes and user actions created in App Studio are marked automatically; others are marked in Dev Studio via Actions > Mark as relevant record, after confirming the rule is guardrail-compliant. Markable types include properties, flows, flow actions, SLAs, data transforms, decision tables and trees, when rules, validate rules, correspondence, paragraphs, notifications, Pulse feed rules, sections, harnesses, views, strategies and proposition filters. The inventory is at Configure > Application > Inventory > Relevant Records, with Show inactive and Show inherited options; relevant records inherit down the class hierarchy.
keyFacts: Three class groups: Work (cases), Integration/Int (connectors), Data (data types).
The Division/Unit class layer is optional and used only when necessary.
Pattern = name prefix, automatic; Directed = explicit parent on the class form.
Search order: pattern parents first, then directed parent, repeat to @baseclass.
Example: .pxCreateOpName in Work-Cover- is reached through directed inheritance.
App Studio-created fields, views, processes and user actions are relevant records automatically.
Manual marking: Actions > Mark as relevant record; verify guardrail compliance first.
An existing Dev Studio SLA appears in App Studio's dropdown only if marked relevant.
Relevant records inherit downward (Insurance-Claims to Insurance-Claims-Auto and -Home).
A relevant proposition filter needs its properties, strategies and when rules relevant for the primary context class.

rows: Automatically from the class name prefix
Explicitly on the class rule form
Functional suitability (Pega Work-, Data-, other apps)

examTraps: Directed is not searched first; pattern parents come first.
App Studio-created fields do not need manual marking as relevant.
Marking as relevant should follow a guardrail check, not precede it blindly.
Division layer is optional, Organization is not.

summary: **Tracer** captures runtime events for troubleshooting; it is not for performance analysis because it has heavy impact. Open it from the App Studio runtime toolbar (lower-right toggle) or the Dev Studio developer toolbar. Event colors: gray for activities, orange for flows, decisions and declaratives, light blue for database and cache. Each event shows Good or Fail, and the real root cause may sit before the final failed step. In Constellation, events are grouped by request ID because the DX API is stateless. One Tracer can run per operator per node.

The toolbar offers Pause, Clear and Save, plus Settings (event types, rulesets, break conditions, number of lines, filters such as removing View rules), Breakpoints (pause the thread on an activity; resume with Play or automatically after one hour), Watch (track property value changes, shown in the Property Inspector with old and current values and a yellow highlight) and Remote Tracer. Breakpoints and Watch are not supported for Service rules or Constellation applications.

For Constellation front ends, other tools help: view rule metadata (JSON when the pxEnableC11nDev when rule is true), browser F12 tools (Console, Network for DX API payloads, Application storage), React DevTools, Redux DevTools (actions, state, time travel), XRay toggled with `PCore.getDebugger().toggleXRay(true)`, the DebugPegaAPI setting for verbose DX API logs, `PCore.getDataPageUtils()` for client-side data pages, and UI Inspector. PCore/PConnect are not available inside the App Studio shell, so launch the portal from Dev Studio.
keyFacts: Tracer is for troubleshooting, not performance analysis.
Colors: gray = activity, orange = flow/decision/declarative, light blue = database and cache.
Root cause can occur before the last failed event.
Constellation events are grouped by request ID.
One Tracer per operator per node.
Breakpoints pause the thread; resume on Play or after one hour.
Watch shows old vs current values in the Property Inspector with yellow highlight.
Breakpoints and Watch are unsupported for Service rules and Constellation apps.
XRay: `PCore.getDebugger().toggleXRay(true/false)`; DebugPegaAPI = true gives verbose DX API logs.
PCore/PConnect are unavailable in the App Studio shell; launch the portal from Dev Studio.
examTraps: Using Tracer to measure performance is wrong; it adds heavy overhead.
Breakpoints do not wait forever; they resume after one hour.
Do not expect Breakpoints/Watch to work for a Constellation app.
The final red Fail line is not necessarily the root cause.

summary: Configuration sets and settings provide a unified framework for parameters that control application behavior, reducing the need for rule overrides and replacing Dynamic System Settings. Typical uses: toggling features (disable outbound email until the integration is finished), steering process paths (an approval monetary limit) and UI behavior (show instructions for a new process). They are managed in App Studio on the Settings tab, Configurations landing page, and referenced via the Condition Builder.

Settings are instances of Data-Configuration-Setting; sets live in the Pega-Configuration class. A set does not appear until it holds at least one setting, and its name (pyLabel) can be up to 64 characters. Access: SysAdm4 can read, write and delete both sets and settings; WorkMgr4 can read/write/delete sets but only read settings; User4 can only read both. They travel in the product file when Include associated data is selected.
keyFacts: Configuration settings replace Dynamic System Settings for app behavior parameters.
Location: App Studio Settings tab > Configurations landing page.
Settings = Data-Configuration-Setting; sets = Pega-Configuration class.
A set is hidden until it contains at least one setting.
Set name (pyLabel) max 64 characters.
Roles: SysAdm4 full on both; WorkMgr4 full on sets, read settings; User4 read only.
Packaged when Include associated data is checked on the product file.
Referenced in logic through the Condition Builder.
examTraps: A newly created empty set not showing is expected behavior, not a bug.
Do not reach for Dynamic System Settings; configuration settings replace them.
WorkMgr4 cannot edit settings, only sets.

questions.stem: A citizen developer builds a Claims Case Type in App Studio. The Assess Damage step needs an SLA that uses a business-days calendar and holds the assignment with a delay timer before it is routed. Which approach follows Pega best practice?
options: Configure the goal and deadline in App Studio, then add the advanced options to the generated SLA rule in Dev Studio.
Configure the business-days calendar and delay timer in the App Studio Goal & deadline settings.
Rebuild the whole Case Type in Dev Studio because one requirement needs it.
Configure the SLA in Admin Studio, where runtime timing is managed.
questions.explanation: Best practice is to build in App Studio and move to Dev Studio only for what App Studio does not expose. App Studio creates an SLA rule behind its Goal & deadline settings, and the business-days calendar and the initialization delay timer are Dev Studio options on that rule. App Studio does not offer either option. Rebuilding the whole Case Type in Dev Studio ignores the App Studio-first practice. Admin Studio is for runtime monitoring by IT system administrators, not for designing SLAs.

questions.stem: A business architect asks a Dev Studio developer to add a new adjuster to the Claims team and to tighten the Goal & deadline on the Review step. Which two Dev Studio records hold these settings?
options: An Access Group and a Service Level Agreement rule
A Work Group and a Service Level Agreement rule
A Work Group and a Decision table
An Access Role and a Flow rule
questions.explanation: In Dev Studio terms, a Team is a Work Group and a Goal & deadline is an SLA (Service Level Agreement) rule, and the adjuster is an Operator (User). An Access Group controls authorization, not team membership. A Decision table holds conditional results, not service levels. An Access Role describes a job function's permissions, and a Flow rule models a Process, so neither one holds team membership or the step's timing.

questions.stem: A global insurer has three layers of shared logic: authentication used by every business line, a claims intake flow reused by its property and auto claims applications, and Germany-only regulatory checks for auto claims. In the Situational Layer Cake, where does the claims intake flow belong?
options: Enterprise layer
Division layer
Application layer
Implementation layer
questions.explanation: The claims intake flow is reused by several applications within one division (claims), so it belongs in the Division layer, which holds division-specific reusable assets. The Enterprise layer is for platform and company-wide assets such as authentication. The Application layer holds rules specific to one application, but this flow is shared by two applications. The Implementation layer holds deployment-specific variations such as the German regulatory checks.

questions.stem: A Center of Excellence is splitting work between professional developers and citizen developers. Under Pega's studio interoperability model, which two tasks belong in Dev Studio? (Choose Two)
options: Marking rules as relevant records for App Studio users
Building reusable modules and automated unit tests
Adjusting application behavior through Configuration Sets
Using relevant records while configuring prescriptive UI
questions.explanation: Dev Studio is where developers build advanced applications, reusable components and modules, automated unit tests and traditional UI, and where they mark rules as relevant records. Configuration Sets are configured in App Studio (Settings tab > Configurations). Using relevant records while building with prescriptive UI is the App Studio side of the model: Dev Studio makes the records available, and App Studio uses them.

questions.stem: Three applications at a bank each need the same meeting-scheduling feature. A developer proposes copying the rules into each application and adding if-then-else conditions for small differences. What is the better modular reuse approach?
options: Package the feature as a module application and add it as a built-on application to each app.
Copy the rules into each application's Implementation layer so each team can edit them.
Mark the rules as relevant records in one application so the other two can see them.
Keep one copy in the first application and branch the logic with When rules for the others.
questions.explanation: Reusable features are delivered as module applications that are stacked as built-on applications, as with the Meeting module example. The Situational Layer Cake exists to avoid both duplicate applications and if-then-else spaghetti. Copying rules into each application duplicates logic. Relevant records make rules visible to App Studio users in an application's own class hierarchy, so they do not share rules across applications. Branching one copy with When rules is the condition-heavy design the Layer Cake avoids.

questions.stem: A bank built its loan application using center-out architecture. This year it moves the customer system of record from on-premises to the cloud and adds a chat channel. Which two outcomes does center-out architecture predict? (Choose Two)
options: The data access layer changes while the loan business logic stays the same.
The chat channel reuses the loan logic that is already defined once at the center.
The chat channel needs its own copy of the eligibility rules to respond correctly.
The business logic is rebuilt to fit the new cloud data structures.
questions.explanation: In center-out architecture, business logic sits in the middle. The data access layer is insulated, so a change of system of record, such as on-premises to cloud, needs no change to the logic. Channels connect from above and reuse the same logic, so it is defined once and the change applies everywhere. A separate copy of the rules per channel describes the top-down approach. Rebuilding logic around data structures reflects the data-centric bottom-up approach.

questions.stem: An organization runs 30 Constellation applications that must meet WCAG 2.1 and Section 508. A new accessibility requirement changes how a common input pattern behaves. Which approach requires the least effort?
options: Update each View that uses the input in all 30 applications.
Update the central UI component so that the change reaches every application.
Save a new theme in each application's Implementation layer with accessible styles.
Run the Themes landing page check in each application and fix the screens it flags.
questions.explanation: Pega generates UI centrally from patterns, so accessibility is implemented once in the central components and propagates to all applications without per-screen changes. Editing each View in 30 applications is the per-screen work that model-driven UI avoids. A theme controls styling, and themes do not support inheritance, so a theme per application does not change how an input pattern behaves. The Themes landing page flags WCAG color-contrast failures only, not input behavior.

questions.stem: During pre-sales, a team co-designed a Blueprint with the client. The deal is signed and a delivery team is formed. Who imports the Blueprint file and configures the functional and technical requirements?
options: Solutions Consultant
Lead System Architect
Business Architect
Product Owner
questions.explanation: The Lead System Architect imports Blueprint files and configures the functional and technical requirements. The Solutions Consultant works in early sales and co-designs the Blueprint, then hands it to the delivery team. The Business Architect turns business needs into functional requirements, workflows, data models and UX, but does not import the Blueprint. The Product Owner is on the client side, defines scope and prioritizes requirements for each sprint.

questions.stem: A new delivery team is writing its RACI chart. Which two role assignments are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Product Owner: prioritizes the requirements for each sprint
Quality Analyst: writes test scripts and scenario tests from user stories
Scrum Master: manages the project budget, schedule and scope
Business Architect: designs the class hierarchy and imports the Blueprint
questions.explanation: The Product Owner represents the client business, defines scope and prioritizes requirements for each sprint. Quality Analysts build test scripts and scenario tests from user stories. Budget, schedule and scope belong to the Project Manager, while the Scrum Master runs the Scrum ceremonies and removes impediments. Designing the class hierarchy and importing Blueprint files is Lead System Architect work. The Business Architect translates business needs into functional requirements.

questions.stem: Developer Maya configured a new View in her workspace for the Onboarding application. A teammate working on the same application cannot see the View. Which statement about Maya's change is correct?
options: It stays private to Maya until she shares it to a Branch.
It is visible to every developer on the application as soon as it is saved.
It is merged into the application rulesets as soon as it is saved.
It is visible to other developers in the same Access Group.
questions.explanation: A workspace is a private development space for one operator and one application. Changes stay private until they are shared (pushed) to a Branch, and the Branch is later merged into the application. Saving does not publish the change to other developers, and it does not skip the Branch and go straight into the application. Membership of an Access Group does not affect what can be seen in another operator's workspace.

questions.stem: A team lead is writing workspace guidance for new developers. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose Two)
options: A workspace is tied to one operator and one application.
An operator can create more than one workspace for the same application.
Each operator is limited to one workspace for each application.
Workspaces are available only in Dev Studio.
questions.explanation: Each workspace belongs to exactly one operator with developer access and to one application. By default each operator has one workspace per application, and more can be created. The statement about a limit of one workspace per application confuses the default with a limit. Workspaces are available in both App Studio and Dev Studio, and they are switched on with the EnableWorkspace setting.

questions.stem: Before approving a merge, a team lead opens the quality metrics for the ClaimsIntake Branch. Which two metrics are reported? (Choose Two)
options: The total number of merge conflicts
The percentage of rules covered and the unit test pass rate
An unweighted count of guardrail warnings
The number of locked ruleset versions in the stack
questions.explanation: Branch quality metrics include the weighted guardrail score, the total number of merge conflicts, test coverage and unit test results (rules covered percentage and test pass rate), and the uncovered rules. The guardrail metric is a weighted score, not an unweighted count of warnings. Locked ruleset versions are a ruleset management practice, not a Branch quality metric.

questions.stem: A team is building the Claims Intake feature and the Payment Calculation feature at the same time. Payment Calculation will take two more sprints. Which Branch strategy follows Pega guidance?
options: Use one Branch for the sprint and merge everything at the end of each sprint.
Use one Branch per developer and merge each Branch daily.
Use one Branch per feature and merge each when it is complete, conflict-free and approved.
Use one Branch per feature and merge each as soon as any rule passes its unit tests.
questions.explanation: Pega recommends one Branch per feature, merged only when the feature is complete, merge conflicts are resolved and the merge is approved. The system also checks for updated or missing rules before merging. A single sprint Branch would push the unfinished Payment Calculation work into the application. A Branch per developer does not separate work by feature. Merging when one rule passes its tests ignores the completion and approval criteria.

questions.stem: During a playback session, one stakeholder says the worklist would be easier to use if it were sorted by due date. Another reports that Submit on the address form saves the wrong postal code. How should the team record these in Agile Workbench?
options: As Feedback for the sorting suggestion and a Bug for the postal code
As Bugs for both, because both came from a playback session
As a user story for the postal code and a Bug for the sorting suggestion
As Feedback for both, because neither was reported in production
questions.explanation: Agile Workbench has three work item types: Stories, Bugs and Feedback. Playbacks are used to capture bugs and feedback from stakeholders. A suggestion about how the worklist should behave is Feedback, and a form that saves an incorrect value is a defect, so it is a Bug. Where an item was found does not decide its type. The postal code problem is not a new user story, and the sorting suggestion is not a defect.

questions.stem: A Product Owner has 80 user stories in a spreadsheet and wants the team to track them in Agile Workbench. Which statement is correct?
options: The stories can be bulk-uploaded from Excel and then tracked through To do, Doing and Done.
Agile Workbench stores only Bugs and Feedback, so the stories must stay in Jira.
Each story must be created by hand because Agile Workbench has no bulk upload.
The stories are imported through the Dev Studio Records explorer.
questions.explanation: Agile Workbench, opened from the App Studio Application profile, supports bulk upload of user stories from Excel. Work items move through To do, Doing and Done, and you drag an item to change its status. Stories are one of its three work item types, and it integrates with Jira rather than relying on it. Bulk upload is supported. The Dev Studio Records explorer is not where Agile Workbench items are managed.

questions.stem: The highest version of ruleset ClaimsMain is 02-03-04, and it is locked. A defect in a calculation must be fixed, with no new functionality. Where should the fix go?
options: ClaimsMain:02-03-05
ClaimsMain:02-04-01
ClaimsMain:03-01-01
Unlock ClaimsMain:02-03-04 and fix it in place
questions.explanation: Ruleset versions use the format major-minor-patch, and bug fixes increment the patch number, so the fix goes in 02-03-05. A minor increment such as 02-04-01 is for enhancements. A major increment such as 03-01-01 is for substantial new functionality or a major platform upgrade. Older versions should stay locked, so unlocking 02-03-04 to change it goes against best practice.

questions.stem: A developer uses Save As on a Decision table, changes only the short description and clicks Create and open. The system shows an error. Which single change allows the copy to be created?
options: Make the short description longer so the label is unique.
Change the Apply to class to a child class.
Check out the original rule before using Save As.
Enable a delegation option on the Results tab.
questions.explanation: Save As pre-fills every key value, and it fails unless the identifier, the Apply to class or the ruleset is changed. Changing the class to a child class meets that requirement and specializes the rule. The short description is not part of the rule's key, so editing it does not help. Checking out the original and setting delegation options do not change the key, so the error remains.

questions.stem: While troubleshooting, a developer reads the `.pzInsKey` of an SLA rule. Which two values make up part of this key? (Choose Two)
options: The internal name of the rule type
The creation timestamp in GMT
The ruleset version that holds the rule
The operator ID of the rule's creator
questions.explanation: `.pzInsKey` combines the internal name of the rule type (such as RULE-OBJ-SERVICELEVEL), the applies-to class, the identifier and the creation timestamp in GMT. Some rule types add more keys, for example the Correspondence type. The ruleset version and the creator's operator ID are not part of the key.

questions.stem: An application's ruleset stack includes the entry ClaimsMain:02-03. Which two ruleset versions does Pega search through this entry? (Choose Two)
options: ClaimsMain:02-01-05
ClaimsMain:02-03-02
ClaimsMain:01-09-09
ClaimsMain:02-04-01
questions.explanation: A ruleset stack entry includes the listed version and every lower minor and patch version within the same major version. That covers 02-03-02 and 02-01-05. Version 01-09-09 belongs to a different major version, so it is outside the entry even though its numbers look higher. Version 02-04-01 is higher than the listed 02-03, so it is not included.

questions.stem: In App Studio, a business architect creates the Employee Relocation Case Type, adds a Process named Pricing and configures a View for one of its steps. Which two Dev Studio rules does this create? (Choose Two)
options: A Flow rule for the Pricing Process
A pyDefault Case Type rule in the Case Type's work class
A Section rule in the Data-Portal class for the View
An Activity rule for each step in the Process
questions.explanation: A new Case Type creates a work class (such as TGB-HRApps-Work-EmployeeRelocation) with a pyDefault Case Type rule, a data page and properties, and each Process becomes a Flow rule. A View does become a Section rule, but its class context is the case class. UI rules in the Data-Portal class come from adding a channel such as Mobile. Steps are not converted into Activity rules.

questions.stem: Class TGB-HR-Work-Relocation uses pattern inheritance and has Work-Cover- as its directed parent. A When rule with the same name is defined in both TGB-HR-Work and Work-Cover-. Which version does rule resolution find first?
options: The TGB-HR-Work version, because pattern parents are searched before the directed parent
The Work-Cover- version, because the directed parent is searched before pattern parents
The version created most recently, regardless of class
Neither, because the same name in two parent classes causes an error
questions.explanation: Rule resolution searches the pattern parents first (by class name prefix, so TGB-HR-Work), then the directed parent and its pattern parents, repeating up to @baseclass. The TGB-HR-Work version is found first. The directed parent comes after the pattern parents, not before. Creation date does not decide which class wins. A rule with the same name at two levels is normal specialization, not an error. An error happens only when no rule is found.

questions.stem: An LSA is explaining class inheritance to new developers. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Pattern inheritance follows the class name prefix automatically.
Directed inheritance is set explicitly on the class rule form.
Directed inheritance reuses rules based on business suitability.
The pattern search stops at the organization class.
questions.explanation: Pattern inheritance is automatic and based on the class name prefix, with hyphens separating levels. Directed inheritance names a parent explicitly on the class rule form, for example to reuse Pega's Work- or Data- classes or rules from other applications. Business suitability describes pattern inheritance, while directed inheritance is about functional suitability. The search does not stop at the organization class: it continues through directed parents up to @baseclass.

questions.stem: A senior developer created an SLA rule in Dev Studio. A citizen developer configuring a step in App Studio cannot find it in the list of existing SLAs. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: The SLA must be marked as a relevant record before App Studio lists it.
The developer should confirm the SLA is guardrail-compliant before marking it.
Only SLAs created in App Studio can appear in the App Studio list.
The SLA is marked as relevant from the SLA list in App Studio.
questions.explanation: An existing Dev Studio SLA appears in App Studio only when it is marked as a relevant record. A developer does this in Dev Studio with Actions > Mark as relevant record, after checking that the rule is guardrail-compliant. SLAs are one of the rule types that can be marked manually, so they are not limited to App Studio-created rules. Marking happens in Dev Studio, not from the App Studio list.

questions.stem: A developer marks a Decision table as a relevant record for class Insurance-Claims. Where can App Studio users see it as relevant?
options: In Insurance-Claims and its child classes, such as Insurance-Claims-Auto and Insurance-Claims-Home
Only in Insurance-Claims, because each child class must mark it separately
In Insurance-Claims and its parent class Insurance
In every class of the application, whatever the hierarchy
questions.explanation: Relevant records inherit down the class hierarchy, so a record marked for Insurance-Claims is relevant in Insurance-Claims-Auto and Insurance-Claims-Home too. Child classes do not need to mark it again. Inheritance runs down the hierarchy, not up to the parent class Insurance. It does not cover classes outside that branch of the hierarchy.

questions.stem: Application TGB-IT has the Case Types TGB-IT-Work-ITTicket and TGB-IT-Work-LaptopRequest. A developer needs a Data Transform that every Case Type in the application can reuse. In which class should it be created?
options: TGB-IT-Work-ITTicket
TGB-IT-Work
TGB-IT-Data-Asset
@baseclass
questions.explanation: Reusable rules should sit as high in the hierarchy as their use allows. TGB-IT-Work is the parent of every Case Type class in the application, so all of them inherit it through pattern inheritance. TGB-IT-Work-ITTicket is a single Case Type, and LaptopRequest is a separate Case Type that does not inherit from it. A Data class holds data types, not case processing. @baseclass is Pega's ultimate base class, which is far too general for application logic.

questions.stem: A developer is debugging a Constellation application. She wants Tracer to pause on a specific activity and to show how a property value changes. What should she expect?
options: Breakpoints and Watch are not supported, and events are grouped by request ID.
A Breakpoint pauses the thread until she clicks Play or one hour passes.
Watch highlights the old and current values in yellow in the Property Inspector.
Tracer cannot be used with Constellation applications.
questions.explanation: Breakpoints and Watch are not supported for Constellation applications or Service rules. Tracer still works, and because the DX API is stateless it groups Constellation events by request ID. The pause-until-Play-or-one-hour behavior and the yellow Old/Current highlighting in the Property Inspector are real features, but they apply only where Breakpoints and Watch are supported. Tracer can still trace Constellation applications.

questions.stem: A developer is reviewing a Tracer session after a case fails to advance. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose Two)
options: Light blue events show database and cache operations.
The root cause can appear in an event before the last failed step.
Orange events show activities.
Tracer is the recommended tool for analyzing performance problems.
questions.explanation: In Tracer, light blue marks database and cache events. The root cause of a failure often appears earlier than the final event marked Fail. Gray marks activities, while orange marks flows, decisions and declaratives. Tracer is for troubleshooting runtime events and has a heavy performance impact, so it is not suited to performance analysis.

questions.stem: A developer opens the browser console while the application is running in the App Studio shell and runs `PCore.getDebugger().toggleXRay(true)`. The command fails because PCore is undefined. What should she do?
options: Set the DebugPegaAPI setting to true and run the command again.
Launch the portal from Dev Studio and run the command there.
Set the pxEnableC11nDev When rule to true.
Turn on Tracer from the Runtime toolbar first.
questions.explanation: PCore and PConnect are not available in the App Studio shell, so the portal must be launched from Dev Studio before running XRay. Setting DebugPegaAPI to true gives verbose DX API logs, but PCore is still undefined. pxEnableC11nDev shows View rule metadata as JSON. Tracer is a separate tool and does not load PCore.

questions.stem: A developer is troubleshooting a Constellation screen with browser and extension tools. Which two tool and purpose pairs are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Browser Network tab: inspect DX API requests and payloads
Redux DevTools: inspect actions and state with time travel
Redux DevTools: inspect client-side data pages
React DevTools Network tab: inspect DX API payloads
questions.explanation: The browser Network tab (Fetch/XHR) shows DX API calls and their payloads. Redux DevTools shows actions and state and supports time travel. Client-side data pages are held in a separate datastore, not in Redux, and are read with `PCore.getDataPageUtils()`. React DevTools is for inspecting components, for example through the Components tab, and has no Network tab for DX API traffic.

questions.stem: A manager with the WorkMgr4 role creates a new configuration set, but cannot change the value of an existing setting. What explains this?
options: WorkMgr4 has full access to configuration sets but read-only access to settings.
Configuration settings can be changed only as Dynamic System Settings in Dev Studio.
A configuration set stays hidden until it contains at least one setting.
Only the User4 role can change configuration settings.
questions.explanation: WorkMgr4 can read, write and delete configuration sets, but can only read settings. SysAdm4 has full access to both, and User4 can only read both. Configuration settings replace Dynamic System Settings and are managed on the Configurations landing page. A set is hidden until it contains a setting, which is true but does not explain why a value cannot be changed. User4 is read-only.
